source_text: Agnosce et mulierem, agnosce et nuptam de testimoniis et corporis et spiritus, quae patitur et in conscientia et in carne. Hae sunt tabellae priores naturalium sponsalium et nuptiarum. Impone velamen extrinsecus habenti tegumen intrinsecus. Tegantur etiam superiora cuius inferiora nuda non sunt. Vis scire quae sit aetatis auctoritas? Propone utramque, immutare compressam in habitu mulieris, et quae maturitate progressa in virginitate duret cum suo habitu: facilius illa mulier negabitur, quam ista virgo credetur. Tanta est adeo fides aetatis, ut nec habitu obstrui possit. Quid? quod etiam hae nostrae etiam habitu mutationem aetatis confitentur, simulque se mulieres intellexerunt, de virginibus educantur, a capite quidem ipso deponentes quod fuerunt: vertunt capillum et acu lasciviore comam sibi inserunt, crinibus a fronte divisis apertam professae mulieritatem. lavacro macerant, formae a speculo petunt, et faciem morosiorem lavacro macerant, forsitan et aliquo eam medicamine interpolant, pallium extrinsecus iactant, calceum stipant multiformem, plus instrumenti ad balneas deferunt. Quid singula persequar? Solae autem manifestae paraturae totam circumferunt mulieritatem, sed virginari volunt sola capitis nuditate, uno habitu negantes quod toto suggestu profitentur.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that a virgin's own body and conduct testify that she is a woman, so she should accept the veil.
pass_a_gloss: Recognize also the woman, recognize also the bride from the testimonies both of body and of spirit, which she suffers both in conscience and in flesh. These are the earlier tablets of natural betrothals and marriages. Impose a veil outwardly on one who has a covering inwardly. Let also the upper parts be covered of her whose lower parts are not bare. Do you wish to know what is the authority of age? Set forth both: to change one who has been pressed into the dress of a woman, and one who, having advanced by maturity, continues in virginity with her own dress: more easily will that one be denied to be a woman, than this one will be believed to be a virgin. So great is the credibility of age, that it cannot be blocked even by dress. What? that even these women of ours also confess by dress the change of age, and as soon as they have understood themselves to be women, they are brought out from among the virgins, from the head itself indeed laying aside what they were: they turn the hair and insert into their hair a pin with rather wanton point, with the hair parted from the forehead they profess womanhood laid open. They soften with washing, they seek beauty from the mirror, and they soften a rather peevish face with washing, perhaps they also touch it up with some cosmetic, they toss the mantle outwardly, they pack a shoe of many forms, they carry more equipment to the baths. Why should I pursue the details? But their open adornments alone carry around the whole of womanhood, but they wish to be virgins by the bareness of the head alone, denying by one dress what they profess by the whole display.

choices.term: tabellae priores naturalium sponsalium et nuptiarum
choices.english: the earlier tablets of natural betrothals and marriages
choices.why: Keeps the legal metaphor of written records or tablets, which Tertullian uses to say the body and spirit already testify to womanhood before any formal betrothal.
rejected: the first documents of natural engagements and weddings
the prior records of natural espousals and marriages

choices.why: Preserves the contrast between inward covering (modesty of conscience) and the outward veil, which is the point of the imperative.
Renders auctoritas as authority, matching the argument that age itself has a decisive, commanding testimony.
Keeps the physical, forceful sense of comprimo, suggesting a woman whose body has been pressed or embraced, as opposed to a virgin.
rejected: a woman who has known a man

choices.why: Renders the rare noun mulieritas literally as womanhood, preserving Tertullian's coinage for the state of being a woman.
Keeps the verbal form virginari, which Tertullian uses to mean 'to act as or be a virgin', matching the contrast with professing womanhood.

pass_b_english: Recognize the woman, and recognize the bride, by the testimony of both body and spirit, by what she endures in conscience and in flesh. These are the earlier records of natural betrothals and marriages. Put the veil on outwardly, since she has a covering inwardly. Let the upper parts be covered too, since the lower parts are not bare. Do you want to know the authority of age? Set both before you: one changed by defloration into a woman's dress, and one who has advanced in maturity and remains in virginity with her own dress. The first will more easily be denied to be a woman than the second will be believed to be a virgin. So great is the testimony of age that not even dress can block it. What then? Even these women of ours confess the change of age by their dress, and as soon as they understand themselves to be women, they are brought out from among the virgins, removing from their heads the sign of what they were. They turn their hair and pin it up with a more wanton pin, parting the hair from the forehead and openly professing womanhood. They soak themselves in the bath, seek beauty from the mirror, and make their face more fastidious by washing, perhaps even touching it up with some cosmetic. They fling a mantle over themselves, cram their feet into elaborate shoes, and carry more equipment to the baths. Why should I pursue every detail? Their visible preparations alone carry their whole womanhood around with them, yet they want to be virgins by the bareness of the head alone, denying with one garment what they profess with their whole display.

problems.quote: one who has been pressed, changed into a woman's dress
problems.why: 'compressam' means 'married/having known a man', not 'pressed'; she is changed by marriage into a woman's dress.
problems.fix: one changed by marriage into a woman's dress
problems.ruling: Latin 'compressam' implies deflowered/married; 'pressed' fails to convey sexual meaning.

edits.old: one who has been pressed, changed into a woman's dress
edits.new: one changed by marriage into a woman's dress

fixed: Corrected 'one who has been pressed, changed into a woman's dress' to 'one changed by marriage into a woman's dress': source 'immutare compressam in habitu mulieris' means 'to change one who has been married into a woman's dress', where 'compressam' refers to having known a man, not being pressed.

problems.quote: one changed by marriage into a woman's dress
problems.why: compressam means 'confined/restrained', not 'by marriage'; it refers to a married woman constrained in a wife's dress.
problems.fix: one confined in a woman's dress by marriage
problems.ruling: Latin 'immutare compressam in habitu mulieris' means 'change the constrained one in a woman's dress', not 'changed by marriage'

edits.old: one changed by marriage into a woman's dress
edits.new: one confined by marriage in a woman's dress

fixed: The English 'one changed by marriage into a woman's dress' misstates 'immutare compressam in habitu mulieris': 'compressam' means 'confined/restrained', not 'changed', and the phrase describes a married woman constrained in a wife's dress. Changed to 'one confined by marriage in a woman's dress'.

problems.quote: laying aside from the head itself what they were
problems.why: Obscure; likely means removing the veil or virgin's hairstyle, but reads as word-for-word.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'removing from their heads the sign of what they were.'

problems.why: 'Wanton needle' is odd; likely means 'elaborate' or 'ostentatious' pin.
problems.fix: Render as 'a more elaborate pin' or 'a more showy pin.'

edits.old: laying aside from the head itself what they were
edits.new: removing from their heads the sign of what they were

fixed: The source 'a capite quidem ipso deponentes quod fuerunt' means they remove from the head the thing that marked their former state (the virgin's head-covering or hairstyle), so 'removing from their heads the sign of what they were' clarifies the obscure literal rendering.

The source 'acu lasciviore' uses 'lasciviore' (comparative of 'lascivus', wanton/playful) to describe the pin, but in English 'wanton needle' is odd; 'elaborate pin' better conveys the ostentatious adornment Tertullian describes.

problems.quote: one confined by marriage in a woman's dress
problems.why: immutare compressam means changed by sexual compression into a woman's dress, not confined by marriage. The verb is dropped.
problems.fix: one changed by compression into a woman's dress
problems.ruling: "compressam" means sexually embraced or possessed, not "confined". The English also drops "immutare", so the sense of a change in the woman is lost.

edits.old: one confined by marriage in a woman's dress
edits.new: one changed by defloration into a woman's dress

fixed: Fixed `one confined by marriage in a woman's dress`: Latin `immutare compressam in habitu mulieris` means changed by sexual pressing/deflowering into a woman's dress, not confinement by marriage; restored `changed/into` and sexual sense.

problems.quote: pin it up with a more elaborate pin
problems.why: lasciviore means more wanton or licentious, not more elaborate; the moral charge is lost.
problems.fix: They turn their hair and fasten it with a more wanton pin.
problems.ruling: "lasciviore" means more wanton, frivolous or sportive. "More elaborate" drops that moral colouring, which fits Tertullian's censure of the new hairstyle.

fixed: Fixed 'more elaborate pin' to 'more wanton pin' for source acu lasciviore, which means wanton/licentious, not elaborate.
